records.source: Τὸν δὲ ἀσθενοῦντα τῇ πίστει προσλαμβάνεσθε, μὴ εἰς διακρίσεις διαλογισμῶν.
records.gloss: Now the [one] being weak in the faith receive, not for disputes of opinions.
pieces: Welcome anyone whose faith is weak, but not in order to quarrel over their opinions.

L.1: Now welcome the one who is weak in faith, not for disputes over opinions.

R.1: Some believers have weak faith. Make them welcome among you, and do not start arguments with them about what they think.

decisions.choice: weak in faith: not yet confident before God that one is free in matters such as food and special days
alternatives: weak in trust in God in general
decisions.reason: The chapter shows what Paul means: the weak eat only vegetables (verse 2) and set some days apart (verse 5). Faith here is the settled conviction before God that a thing is allowed (verses 22-23). It is not a verdict on their standing with God, for God has welcomed them (verse 3).

decisions.choice: the weak were most likely keeping Jewish food laws and holy days
alternatives: ascetic avoidance of meat and wine from outside Judaism
fear of meat that had been offered to idols (as in 1 Corinthians 8)
decisions.reason: Paul calls food "unclean" with κοινός (verse 14), the word of Jewish purity law (Mark 7:2; Acts 10:14), and he ends the argument by speaking of Jews and Gentiles together (15:7-12). But he never names the group, and avoiding meat and wine was not itself required by the law, so the exact background is uncertain.

decisions.choice: disputes over opinions
decisions.reason: διάκρισις is a deciding between views, here a quarrel; διαλογισμός is a person's thoughts or reasonings. Welcome them, but not so as to argue down their views.

decisions.choice: welcome
decisions.reason: προσλαμβάνομαι is to take someone into your company and fellowship. The same verb says that God has welcomed the person (verse 3) and that the Messiah welcomed you (15:7), so it is "welcome" each time.

decisions.choice: whose faith is weak; some believers
decisions.reason: The Greek says "the one who is weak in faith", a type of person. Balanced and Readable say "anyone" or "some believers" so that the sentence reads naturally.

records.heading: The weak and the strong

records.source: ὃς μὲν πιστεύει φαγεῖν πάντα, ὁ δὲ ἀσθενῶν λάχανα ἐσθίει.
records.gloss: One indeed believes to eat all things, but the [one] being weak eats vegetables.
pieces: One person believes it is right to eat anything, while another, who is weak, eats only vegetables.

L.2: One person believes [he may] eat all things, but the one who is weak eats vegetables.

R.2: One person believes it is all right to eat any kind of food. Another person, whose faith is weak, eats only vegetables.

decisions.choice: believes: has the conviction before God that eating anything is allowed
decisions.reason: πιστεύω with "to eat" is the confidence that a thing is permitted. It is the verb of the noun "faith" in verses 1, 22 and 23, and the strong person's freedom comes from that faith.

decisions.choice: the weak person avoids meat altogether
decisions.reason: Eating vegetables is set against eating everything, so it means eating no meat (verse 21 names meat and wine). Paul does not say why. Jews living among Gentiles sometimes kept off meat that could not be known to be clean, as Daniel and his friends did (Daniel 1:8-16).

decisions.choice: only vegetables
decisions.reason: The contrast with "anything" shows that the weak eat vegetables and nothing else; Balanced and Readable add "only" to make that plain.

decisions.choice: it is right / it is all right
decisions.reason: Literal supplies "he may" in brackets. Balanced and Readable say "it is right" or "it is all right", which needs no pronoun for a person who may be a man or a woman.

records.source: ὁ ἐσθίων τὸν μὴ ἐσθίοντα μὴ ἐξουθενείτω, ὁ δὲ μὴ ἐσθίων τὸν ἐσθίοντα μὴ κρινέτω, ὁ θεὸς γὰρ αὐτὸν προσελάβετο.
records.gloss: The [one] eating the [one] not eating let not despise, and the [one] not eating the [one] eating let not judge, for the God him received.
pieces: The one who eats must not look down on the one who abstains, and the one who abstains must not pass judgment on the one who eats, because God has welcomed that person.

L.3: The one who eats must not look down on the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat must not judge the one who eats, for God has welcomed {{gender:them|him}}.

R.3: If you eat meat, do not look down on people who do not. If you do not eat meat, do not judge people who do. God has welcomed them.

decisions.choice: look down on / judge: the typical fault of each side
decisions.reason: The strong are tempted to despise (ἐξουθενέω) the weak as narrow; the weak are tempted to judge (κρίνω), that is, condemn, the strong as sinners. Paul forbids both, and asks the same two questions again in verse 10.

decisions.choice: him: the one who eats
alternatives: both the eater and the abstainer
decisions.reason: The pronoun follows "the one who eats", the person the abstainer condemns, and God's welcome answers that condemnation. Paul says elsewhere that both are welcomed (15:7), but this sentence speaks of the eater.

decisions.choice: abstains
decisions.reason: Balanced says "abstains" for "does not eat", which is clear in context and avoids repeating "eat" four times.

decisions.choice: meat
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "eat" and "not eat". Verse 2 and verse 21 show that the food in question is meat, so Readable names it.

records.source: σὺ τίς εἶ ὁ κρίνων ἀλλότριον οἰκέτην;
records.gloss: You, who are you, the [one] judging another's household servant?
pieces: Who are you to judge someone else's servant?

L.4: Who are you, the one who judges another's household servant?

R.4: Who are you to judge a servant who belongs to someone else?

decisions.choice: household servant
decisions.reason: οἰκέτης is a servant of a household, usually a slave. The word stresses whose household the servant belongs to, which is Paul's point: the servant answers to the master, not to you.

decisions.choice: a picture from household life
decisions.reason: Nobody had the right to discipline another person's servant. The believer you are judging belongs to the Lord, as the next sentence and verses 7-9 say.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: The project says "slave" for the usual word for a slave (1:1), but this is a different word, chosen for the household picture; "servant" keeps the two words apart.

records.source: τῷ ἰδίῳ κυρίῳ στήκει ἢ πίπτει· σταθήσεται δέ, δυνατεῖ γὰρ ὁ κύριος στῆσαι αὐτόν.
records.gloss: To the own master he stands or falls; but he will be made to stand, for able is the Lord to make stand him.
pieces: It is to their own master that they stand or fall. And they will stand, because the Lord has the power to keep them standing.

L.4: To {{gender:their|his}} own master {{gender:they stand|he stands}} or {{gender:fall|falls}}; and {{gender:they|he}} will be made to stand, for the Lord is able to make {{gender:them|him}} stand.

R.4: Whether that servant does well or fails is up to the master, not you. And the servant will stand firm, because the Lord is able to hold them up.

decisions.choice: master, then Lord: the picture turns to Christ
decisions.reason: κύριος means the owner of a servant and also "the Lord". Paul begins with the household picture and ends by speaking of the Lord himself, who is Christ, Lord of the dead and the living (verses 8-9).

decisions.choice: stands or falls: is approved or not; will be made to stand: will be upheld
alternatives: is acquitted or condemned at the last judgment
decisions.reason: Standing and falling is the servant's standing in the master's eyes. The passive "will be made to stand", with the Lord's power as the reason, says that the Lord will keep this believer standing; judgment comes in verse 10.

decisions.choice: the Lord
decisions.reason: Some later manuscripts read "God" (θεός) here instead of "the Lord". The SBLGNT follows the earliest manuscripts. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: they / their / them for the servant
decisions.reason: The servant stands for any believer, man or woman. Balanced and Readable use "they" for one person; Literal keeps "he" as a gender setting.

decisions.choice: is up to the master, not you
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain the point of "to their own master": the servant answers to the master, not to the one judging.

records.source: Ὃς μὲν κρίνει ἡμέραν παρ’ ἡμέραν, ὃς δὲ κρίνει πᾶσαν ἡμέραν· ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω·
records.gloss: One indeed judges a day beyond a day, but another judges every day; each in the own mind let be fully convinced;
pieces: One person regards one day as more important than another, while someone else regards every day as the same. Each person must be fully convinced in their own mind.

L.5: One person judges one day above another day, but another judges every day [alike]; let each be fully convinced in {{gender:their|his}} own mind;

R.5: Some people think one day is more special than the others. Other people think every day is the same. Each person should be sure in their own mind about what is right.

decisions.choice: special days: most likely the Sabbath and the Jewish feasts and fasts
decisions.reason: Paul does not name the days. Coming beside food that some call "unclean" (verse 14), the Sabbath and the festivals of the law are the most likely (Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16).

decisions.choice: judges: considers, rates
decisions.reason: κρίνω is the same verb as "judge" in verses 3, 4, 10 and 13. Here it means to rate one day above another; Paul plays on its senses through the chapter.

decisions.choice: fully convinced
decisions.reason: πληροφορέω is to be fully assured. Each believer should act from a settled conviction before the Lord, which verse 23 calls faith.

decisions.choice: judges
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "judges" so that the reader can see the same verb as in verses 3, 4, 10 and 13.

decisions.choice: about what is right
decisions.reason: Readable says what each person is to be sure of.

records.source: ὁ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν κυρίῳ φρονεῖ.
records.gloss: The [one] regarding the day to [the] Lord regards [it].
pieces: Whoever observes the day does so for the Lord.

L.6: The one who observes the day observes [it] for [the] Lord.

R.6: People who keep a special day do it to honor the Lord.

decisions.choice: for the Lord: in the Lord's honor and service
decisions.reason: The dative says for whom the day is kept. Both sides act as servants of the same Lord (verse 4), so neither may condemn the other.

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT text
alternatives: later manuscripts add "and the one who does not observe the day does not observe it for the Lord"
decisions.reason: The earliest manuscripts do not have the added clause, which fills out the pattern of the sentences about eating. It is in many later manuscripts and in the printed Greek editions of the sixteenth century. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: to honor the Lord
decisions.reason: Readable says what "for the Lord" means.

records.source: καὶ ὁ ἐσθίων κυρίῳ ἐσθίει, εὐχαριστεῖ γὰρ τῷ θεῷ· καὶ ὁ μὴ ἐσθίων κυρίῳ οὐκ ἐσθίει, καὶ εὐχαριστεῖ τῷ θεῷ.
records.gloss: And the [one] eating to [the] Lord eats, for he gives thanks to the God; and the [one] not eating to [the] Lord not eats, and gives thanks to the God.
pieces: Those who eat do so for the Lord, since they give thanks to God; and those who abstain do so for the Lord, and they too give thanks to God.

L.6: And the one who eats, eats for [the] Lord, for {{gender:they give|he gives}} thanks to God; and the one who does not eat, for [the] Lord does not eat, and gives thanks to God.

R.6: People who eat meat do it to honor the Lord, because they thank God for their food. People who do not eat meat also do it to honor the Lord, and they thank God too.

decisions.choice: giving thanks: the thanksgiving said over a meal
decisions.reason: Jews and Christians gave thanks to God before eating (1 Corinthians 10:30; 1 Timothy 4:3-5). The one who eats and the one who abstains both thank God, so both are acting before God.

decisions.choice: for the Lord
decisions.reason: As in the first half of the verse, the dative says for whom each one acts.

decisions.choice: those who eat / those who abstain
alternatives: the one who eats / the one who does not eat
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn the general singular into a plural, which reads naturally and needs no "he".

decisions.choice: meat; for their food
decisions.reason: As in verse 3, Readable names the food in question, which verses 2 and 21 show is meat, and says what the thanks is for.

records.source: Οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἡμῶν ἑαυτῷ ζῇ, καὶ οὐδεὶς ἑαυτῷ ἀποθνῄσκει·
records.gloss: For no one of us to himself lives, and no one to himself dies;
pieces: For not one of us lives for ourselves, and not one of us dies for ourselves.

L.7: For none of us lives to {{gender:themselves|himself}}, and no one dies to {{gender:themselves|himself}};

R.7: None of us lives only for ourselves, and none of us dies only for ourselves.

decisions.choice: to oneself: as one's own master
decisions.reason: The contrast in the next verse is "to the Lord". Paul does not mean that people depend on each other, true as that is, but that no believer belongs to themselves: life and death are both lived for the Lord.

decisions.choice: only
decisions.reason: Readable adds "only" so that the sentence does not seem to say that believers gain nothing themselves; the point is whom they live for.

records.source: ἐάν τε γὰρ ζῶμεν, τῷ κυρίῳ ζῶμεν, ἐάν τε ἀποθνῄσκωμεν, τῷ κυρίῳ ἀποθνῄσκομεν.
records.gloss: For both if we live, to the Lord we live, and if we die, to the Lord we die.
pieces: If we live, we live for the Lord; if we die, we die for the Lord.

L.8: For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord.

R.8: If we live, we live for the Lord. If we die, we die for the Lord.

decisions.choice: to the Lord: for the Lord, as belonging to him
decisions.reason: The dative is the same as in verse 6. Every part of a believer's life, and even death, is for the Lord.

decisions.choice: for the Lord
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "to the Lord" as in the Greek; Balanced and Readable say "for the Lord", which says plainly what the dative means.

records.source: ἐάν τε οὖν ζῶμεν ἐάν τε ἀποθνῄσκωμεν, τοῦ κυρίου ἐσμέν.
records.gloss: If both therefore we live, if also we die, of the Lord we are.
pieces: So, living or dying, we belong to the Lord.

L.8: So whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.

R.8: So whether we are alive or dead, we belong to the Lord.

decisions.choice: the Lord's: belonging to the Lord
decisions.reason: The genitive is of ownership, as a servant belongs to a master (verse 4). This is the conclusion of verses 7-8.

records.source: εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ Χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν καὶ ἔζησεν ἵνα καὶ νεκρῶν καὶ ζώντων κυριεύσῃ.
records.gloss: For to this Christ died and lived, that both of dead and of living he might be lord.
pieces: This is why {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} died and came to life: so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would be Lord of both the dead and the living.

L.9: For to this [end] {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} died and lived [again], so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} might be Lord of both [the] dead and [the] living.

R.9: {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} died and came back to life for this reason: to be Lord over both the dead and the living.

decisions.choice: lived: came to life again, his resurrection
decisions.reason: The order is "died and lived", so the living comes after the death: it is the resurrection. Revelation 2:8 uses the same verb in the same way: "who was dead and came to life".

decisions.choice: be Lord: rule as Lord
decisions.reason: κυριεύω is formed from κύριος, "Lord". Christ's death and resurrection made him Lord of all his people, those who have died and those who are alive, which is why "we are the Lord's" (verse 8).

decisions.choice: died and lived
alternatives: later manuscripts read "died and rose and lived again" or similar
decisions.reason: The earliest manuscripts have two verbs; later ones vary, adding "rose" or changing "lived" to "lived again", to make the reference to the resurrection explicit. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: lived [again] / came to life
decisions.reason: The verb is simply "lived", but here it means returning to life after death (m1), which Literal shows with a bracketed "again".

records.source: Σὺ δὲ τί κρίνεις τὸν ἀδελφόν σου;
records.gloss: But you, why judge you the brother of you?
pieces: You, then, why do you pass judgment on your {{gender:brother or sister|brother}}?

L.10: But you, why do you judge your {{gender:brother or sister|brother}}?

R.10: You who do not eat meat, why do you judge a fellow believer?

decisions.choice: you: the one who abstains
decisions.reason: The two questions of this verse answer the two faults of verse 3: the abstainer judges, the eater looks down. This first "you" is the abstainer.

decisions.choice: brother: a fellow believer, man or woman
decisions.reason: ἀδελφός is a member of the family of believers.

decisions.choice: You who do not eat meat
decisions.reason: Readable says which person Paul is addressing (m1).

records.heading: We will all stand before God

records.source: ἢ καὶ σὺ τί ἐξουθενεῖς τὸν ἀδελφόν σου;
records.gloss: Or also you, why despise you the brother of you?
pieces: Or you, why do you look down on your {{gender:brother or sister|brother}}?

L.10: Or you also, why do you look down on your {{gender:brother or sister|brother}}?

R.10: And you who eat anything, why do you look down on a fellow believer?

decisions.choice: you: the one who eats
decisions.reason: The second question is put to the one who eats, whom verse 3 told not to look down on the abstainer.

decisions.choice: you who eat anything
decisions.reason: Readable says which person Paul is addressing (m1).

records.source: πάντες γὰρ παραστησόμεθα τῷ βήματι τοῦ θεοῦ, γέγραπται γάρ· Ζῶ ἐγώ, λέγει κύριος, ὅτι ἐμοὶ κάμψει πᾶν γόνυ, καὶ πᾶσα γλῶσσα ἐξομολογήσεται τῷ θεῷ.
records.gloss: For all we will stand before the judgment seat of the God, \v 11 for it has been written: Live I, says [the] Lord, that to me will bow every knee, and every tongue will confess to the God.
pieces: We will all stand before God's judgment seat.
For it is written: "As I live, says the Lord, every knee will bend before {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and every tongue will openly acknowledge God."

L.10: For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God,
L.11: for it is written: "[As] I live, says [the] Lord, every knee will bow to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and every tongue will confess to God."

R.10: All of us will stand in front of God to be judged.
R.11: Scripture says, "As surely as I live, says the Lord, everyone will kneel down before {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and everyone will openly honor God."

decisions.choice: Isaiah 45:23, introduced by the oath "As I live, says the Lord" (as in Isaiah 49:18)
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 45:23 God swears that every knee will bow to him and every tongue will swear allegiance. Paul opens with the oath found in Isaiah 49:18 and elsewhere. The Greek has "Lord" (κύριος), where the Hebrew of Isaiah has the divine name. Philippians 2:10-11 applies the same words to Jesus.

decisions.choice: the judgment seat of God
decisions.reason: The βῆμα was the raised platform where a ruler or judge gave verdicts. Every believer, strong and weak, will answer to God; that is why they must not judge one another now. 2 Corinthians 5:10 calls it the judgment seat of Christ.

decisions.choice: of God
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "of Christ", probably under the influence of 2 Corinthians 5:10. The earliest manuscripts and the SBLGNT read "of God". (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: acknowledge openly, giving God the honor due
decisions.reason: ἐξομολογέω is to declare openly. In Isaiah every tongue swears loyalty to God; here, with the judgment in view, every person will openly acknowledge God as God. The same verb means praise in 15:9.

decisions.choice: every knee, every tongue: every person, in submission and in speech
decisions.reason: Bowing the knee is submission to a king; the tongue stands for what a person says. Together they mean every person, wholly.

decisions.choice: [As] I live / As I live / As surely as I live
decisions.reason: "I live" is the form of an oath in which God swears by his own life. Literal supplies "As" in brackets, Balanced says "As I live", and Readable "As surely as I live".

decisions.choice: Scripture says
decisions.reason: As in Romans 1:17, Readable says "Scripture says" for "it is written".

decisions.choice: everyone will kneel down; everyone will openly honor God
alternatives: every knee will bow; every tongue will confess
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of knee and tongue (m5).

decisions.choice: the sentence is split in two
decisions.reason: The quotation is the ground for the statement before it; Balanced and Readable start a new sentence with it.

records.source: ἄρα ἕκαστος ἡμῶν περὶ ἑαυτοῦ λόγον δώσει.
records.gloss: So each of us concerning himself account will give.
pieces: So each of us will have to give an account of ourselves.

L.12: So then each of us will give an account concerning {{gender:themselves|himself}}.

R.12: So every one of us will have to answer for our own life.

decisions.choice: give an account: answer for oneself
decisions.reason: To give an account (λόγος) was what a steward or servant did before the master. Each believer will answer for their own life, not for another's.

decisions.choice: the sentence ends with "will give"
decisions.reason: Some important early manuscripts end the sentence without "to God"; many others, early and late, have it. The SBLGNT leaves it out. The sense is the same, since verse 10 has just named God's judgment seat. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

records.source: Μηκέτι οὖν ἀλλήλους κρίνωμεν· ἀλλὰ τοῦτο κρίνατε μᾶλλον, τὸ μὴ τιθέναι πρόσκομμα τῷ ἀδελφῷ ἢ σκάνδαλον.
records.gloss: No longer therefore one another let us judge; but this judge rather, the not to put a stumbling block to the brother or a trap.
pieces: So let us stop judging one another. Use your judgment for this instead: never to put a stumbling block or a snare in the way of a {{gender:brother or sister|brother}}.

L.13: Therefore let us no longer judge one another; but rather judge this: not to put a stumbling block or a trap before [your] {{gender:brother or sister|brother}}.

R.13: So we should stop judging each other. Instead, make up your mind about this: never do anything that would make a fellow believer trip and fall.

decisions.choice: a play on "judge": stop judging others, and judge (decide) this instead
decisions.reason: κρίνω is used twice in two senses: to condemn and to decide. Paul turns the habit of judging one another into a decision about one's own conduct.

decisions.choice: stumbling block / trap: something that leads a fellow believer into sin
alternatives: something that merely offends or annoys
decisions.reason: πρόσκομμα is an obstacle to trip over and σκάνδαλον the trigger of a trap. Verses 20-23 show what is meant: a believer is led to eat against their conscience, which is sin, and their faith is damaged.

decisions.choice: judge ... judge this / judging ... use your judgment
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the play on the word (m1). Readable says "make up your mind" for the second use.

decisions.choice: trip and fall
decisions.reason: Readable turns the two pictures into one plain image.

records.heading: Do not make another believer stumble

records.source: οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι ἐν κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ ὅτι οὐδὲν κοινὸν δι’ ἑαυτοῦ· εἰ μὴ τῷ λογιζομένῳ τι κοινὸν εἶναι, ἐκείνῳ κοινόν.
records.gloss: I know and I am persuaded in [the] Lord Jesus that nothing [is] unclean through itself; except to the [one] reckoning anything unclean to be, to that one [it is] unclean.
pieces: I know, and in the Lord Jesus I am fully persuaded, that nothing is unclean in itself. But if someone considers a thing unclean, then for that person it is unclean.

L.14: I know and am persuaded in [the] Lord Jesus that nothing [is] unclean in itself; except that to the one who considers anything to be unclean, to that one [it is] unclean.

R.14: I belong to the Lord Jesus, and I know for sure that no food is unclean in itself. But if someone thinks a food is unclean, then it is unclean for them.

decisions.choice: unclean: forbidden by the purity laws
decisions.reason: κοινός means "common", and in Jewish use what is ritually unclean and not to be eaten (Mark 7:2; Acts 10:14). Paul declares that no food is unclean in itself.

decisions.choice: in the Lord Jesus: as one who belongs to the Lord, persuaded on his authority
alternatives: persuaded by a saying of Jesus himself (Mark 7:15-19)
decisions.reason: Paul's certainty rests on his union with the Lord Jesus. He may also be thinking of Jesus' own teaching that what goes into a person does not make them unclean (Mark 7:15-19), but he does not quote it.

decisions.choice: except: unclean to the person who thinks it so
decisions.reason: The exception does not change what is true of the food. It says that a person who believes a food is unclean sins by eating it, because they act against their conscience (verse 23).

decisions.choice: no food; a food
decisions.reason: The Greek says "nothing" and "anything". The chapter is about food, so Readable names it.

decisions.choice: I belong to the Lord Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable explains "in the Lord Jesus" (m2) as belonging to him.

records.source: εἰ γὰρ διὰ βρῶμα ὁ ἀδελφός σου λυπεῖται, οὐκέτι κατὰ ἀγάπην περιπατεῖς.
records.gloss: For if because of food the brother of you is grieved, no longer according to love are you walking.
pieces: If your {{gender:brother or sister|brother}} is being hurt by what you eat, you are no longer walking in the way of love.

L.15: For if because of food your {{gender:brother or sister|brother}} is grieved, you are no longer walking according to love.

R.15: If what you eat is hurting a fellow believer, you are not acting in love anymore.

decisions.choice: is grieved: is hurt, deeply distressed
decisions.reason: λυπέω is real grief or pain, not mild annoyance. The weaker believer may be distressed by seeing the strong eat, or drawn into eating against conscience; the next sentence speaks of being destroyed.

decisions.choice: walk: live, behave
decisions.reason: To walk is a common picture for the way a person lives (6:4; 8:4; 13:13).

decisions.choice: by what you eat
decisions.reason: The food is the eater's own food, as the next sentence says ("your food").

records.source: μὴ τῷ βρώματί σου ἐκεῖνον ἀπόλλυε ὑπὲρ οὗ Χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν.
records.gloss: Not with the food of you that one destroy for whom Christ died.
pieces: Do not let what you eat bring ruin on someone for whom {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} died.

L.15: Do not by your food destroy that one for whom {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} died.

R.15: {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} died for that person. Do not ruin them over what you eat!

decisions.choice: destroy: bring to spiritual ruin
decisions.reason: ἀπόλλυμι is to destroy or ruin. Paul sets the believer's food against the death of Christ for the same person. He means real harm to that person's faith; how far that ruin could go, he does not say here.

decisions.choice: with your food: by means of what you eat
decisions.reason: The dative is the means. The command is to the one who eats.

decisions.choice: bring ruin on
decisions.reason: Balanced says "bring ruin on", which suits harm done to a person's faith; Literal keeps "destroy".

decisions.choice: the reason comes first
decisions.reason: Readable puts "the Messiah died for that person" first, in its own sentence, so that the command that follows carries its full weight.

records.source: μὴ βλασφημείσθω οὖν ὑμῶν τὸ ἀγαθόν.
records.gloss: Not let be slandered therefore of you the good.
pieces: So do not let the good thing you have be slandered.

L.16: Therefore do not let your good be spoken of as evil.

R.16: You are free to eat. That is a good thing. But do not use it in a way that makes people speak badly of it.

decisions.choice: your good: the freedom the strong have in Christ
alternatives: the good things of the gospel that all believers share
decisions.reason: ἀγαθός most likely means the freedom to eat anything, which is good in itself (verse 14). The "your" is plural, though, and some take "the good" to be the blessings of the gospel (as in verse 17) shared by the whole church.

decisions.choice: be slandered: be spoken of as evil
decisions.reason: βλασφημέω is to speak abusively of. It may be the weak who call the freedom sin, or outsiders who see believers quarrel over food; Paul does not say.

decisions.choice: You are free to eat. That is a good thing.
decisions.reason: Readable states what "your good" most likely refers to (m1). As m1 says, this is not certain.

records.source: οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ βρῶσις καὶ πόσις, ἀλλὰ δικαιοσύνη καὶ εἰρήνη καὶ χαρὰ ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ·
records.gloss: For not is the kingdom of the God eating and drinking, but righteousness and peace and joy in [the] Spirit Holy;
pieces: For the kingdom of God is not about eating and drinking. It is righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

L.17: For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness and peace and joy in [the] Holy Spirit;

R.17: God's kingdom is not about what we eat or drink. It is about righteousness, peace and joy that come from the Holy Spirit.

decisions.choice: the kingdom of God: God's reign, already present among believers
decisions.reason: Paul speaks of what God's kingdom is now: what it consists of in the life of the church. It is not marked out by rules about food and drink.

decisions.choice: righteousness: right living toward God and others
alternatives: the gift of right standing with God (as in 1:17)
decisions.reason: Beside peace and joy, and in a passage about how believers treat each other, righteousness is most likely right conduct. In Romans the word often means God's gift of right standing, and the two cannot be fully separated.

decisions.choice: in the Holy Spirit: produced by the Spirit, and applies to all three
decisions.reason: The phrase may go with joy alone, but righteousness, peace and joy are all the Spirit's work in believers (8:4-6; Galatians 5:22).

decisions.choice: that come from the Holy Spirit
decisions.reason: Readable says what "in the Holy Spirit" means (m3).

records.source: ὁ γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ δουλεύων τῷ Χριστῷ εὐάρεστος τῷ θεῷ καὶ δόκιμος τοῖς ἀνθρώποις.
records.gloss: The [one] for in this serving the Christ [is] well-pleasing to the God and approved to the men.
pieces: Anyone who serves {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} in this way pleases God and wins the approval of others.

L.18: For the one who in this serves the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} [is] pleasing to God and approved by {{gender:people|men}}.

R.18: Anyone who serves {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} like this pleases God, and other people think well of them too.

decisions.choice: in this: in this way, living by righteousness, peace and joy
decisions.reason: "This" most naturally sums up verse 17: serving Christ by the righteousness, peace and joy the Spirit gives.

decisions.choice: in this
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts have the plural "in these things"; the earliest have the singular. The sense is much the same. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: serve as a slave
decisions.reason: δουλεύω is the verb of the word for a slave: to serve someone as one who belongs to them, as believers belong to the Lord (verse 8).

decisions.choice: approved: thought well of after testing
decisions.reason: δόκιμος is what has been tested and found genuine. Such a believer earns the respect of other people, inside and outside the church.

decisions.choice: serves
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "serves"; the idea of belonging to Christ is clear from verses 7-9.

records.source: ἄρα οὖν τὰ τῆς εἰρήνης διώκωμεν καὶ τὰ τῆς οἰκοδομῆς τῆς εἰς ἀλλήλους.
records.gloss: So then the [things] of the peace let us pursue and the [things] of the building up of the toward one another.
pieces: So let us pursue whatever makes for peace and whatever builds one another up.

L.19: So then let us pursue the things of peace and the things of building up for one another.

R.19: So let us work hard at whatever brings peace and whatever helps each other grow stronger.

decisions.choice: let us pursue
decisions.reason: The manuscripts are divided between the exhortation "let us pursue" and the statement "we pursue", which differ by one letter in Greek. The SBLGNT reads "let us pursue", which fits the commands around it. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: building up
decisions.reason: οἰκοδομή is the building of a house. Paul uses it for helping other believers grow in faith and love (15:2; 1 Corinthians 14:12). Verse 20 continues the picture: do not tear down what God is building.

decisions.choice: work hard at
decisions.reason: διώκω is to chase after; Readable says "work hard at".

records.source: μὴ ἕνεκεν βρώματος κατάλυε τὸ ἔργον τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: Not for the sake of food tear down the work of the God.
pieces: Do not pull down God's work just for the sake of food.

L.20: Do not for the sake of food tear down the work of God.

R.20: Do not wreck what God is building just because of food.

decisions.choice: the work of God: the fellow believer, and the church, that God is building
alternatives: the work of faith in a believer's life
decisions.reason: καταλύω is to tear down a building, the opposite of the building up in verse 19. The work of God is what God has built: the weaker believer, for whom Christ died (verse 15), and the church made of such people.

decisions.choice: what God is building
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the building picture of verses 19-20 (m1).

decisions.choice: just
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "just" to bring out the contrast between food and God's work.

records.source: πάντα μὲν καθαρά, ἀλλὰ κακὸν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ τῷ διὰ προσκόμματος ἐσθίοντι.
records.gloss: All things indeed [are] clean, but [it is] evil to the person, the [one] through stumbling eating.
pieces: All food is clean, it is true, but it is wrong for anyone to eat in a way that makes another stumble.

L.20: All things [are] indeed clean, but [it is] wrong for the {{gender:person|man}} who eats through a stumbling block.

R.20: All food is clean. But it is wrong to eat something if it makes another believer stumble.

decisions.choice: all things are clean: all food may be eaten
decisions.reason: καθαρός is ritually clean. This repeats verse 14, and recalls Jesus declaring all foods clean (Mark 7:19).

decisions.choice: eating that makes another stumble: the strong person's eating
alternatives: eating with a stumbling conscience: the weak person who eats against their own conscience
decisions.reason: "Through a stumbling block" can describe the effect of the eating on someone else, as verse 21 has it, or the state of the one who eats, unsure and stumbling, as verse 23 has it. The command in verse 20a and the next verse are addressed to the strong, so this reading is preferred, but both are possible.

decisions.choice: all food
decisions.reason: The Greek has "all things"; the subject is food, as in verse 14.

records.source: καλὸν τὸ μὴ φαγεῖν κρέα μηδὲ πιεῖν οἶνον μηδὲ ἐν ᾧ ὁ ἀδελφός σου προσκόπτει ἢ σκανδαλίζεται ἢ ἀσθενεῖ·
records.gloss: Good the not to eat meat nor to drink wine nor in which the brother of you stumbles or is caused to fall or is weak;
pieces: It is right not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything else that makes your {{gender:brother or sister|brother}} stumble or fall or become weak.

L.21: [It is] good not to eat meat nor to drink wine nor [to do anything] by which your {{gender:brother or sister|brother}} stumbles or is made to fall or is weakened;

R.21: The right thing to do is to give up meat or wine, or anything else, if it makes a fellow believer stumble or fall or grow weak.

decisions.choice: nor anything by which: a general rule after two examples
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves out the verb: "nor in which". It means "nor to do anything by which".

decisions.choice: wine: some avoided it as well as meat
decisions.reason: Paul has not mentioned wine before. Some Jews avoided Gentile wine, which might have been offered to idols (Daniel 1:8). Paul does not say why the weak abstained.

decisions.choice: stumbles or is made to fall or is weakened
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts have only "stumbles"; others, early and late, add "or is made to fall or is weakened". The SBLGNT has the longer text. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: good: right, the better course
decisions.reason: καλός here is what is right and fitting to do.

records.source: σὺ πίστιν ἣν ἔχεις κατὰ σεαυτὸν ἔχε ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: You faith which you have, according to yourself have before the God.
pieces: Whatever faith you have about these things, keep it between yourself and God.

L.22: The faith that you have, keep to yourself before God.

R.22: Your faith about these things is between you and God, so keep it to yourself.

decisions.choice: faith: the conviction, held before God, of what one is free to do
decisions.reason: As in verses 1-2 and 23, faith here is the strong believer's confidence that eating anything is allowed. It is real faith, held before God, but it need not be displayed to the harm of others.

decisions.choice: the faith that you have
alternatives: Do you have faith? Keep it to yourself before God
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts lack the word "that", making the first words a question. The earliest manuscripts have it, as the SBLGNT does. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: about these things
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what faith is meant (m1), so that the sentence is not read as telling believers to keep their faith in Christ secret.

records.source: μακάριος ὁ μὴ κρίνων ἑαυτὸν ἐν ᾧ δοκιμάζει·
records.gloss: Blessed [is] the [one] not judging himself in what he approves;
pieces: Blessed are those who do not condemn themselves by what they approve.

L.22: Blessed [is] the one who does not judge {{gender:themselves|himself}} in what {{gender:they approve|he approves}};

R.22: God blesses people who can do what they have decided is right without having to condemn themselves for it.

decisions.choice: blessed: favored by God
decisions.reason: μακάριος is the word of the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-11) and of 4:7-8: a person on whom God's favor rests.

decisions.choice: not judge oneself in what one approves: have a clear conscience about what one has decided to do
decisions.reason: δοκιμάζω is to test and approve. The blessed person has tested a practice, judged it allowed, and can do it without self-condemnation. The contrast is the doubter of verse 23.

decisions.choice: God blesses
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who blesses, which "blessed" implies.

records.source: ὁ δὲ διακρινόμενος ἐὰν φάγῃ κατακέκριται, ὅτι οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως· πᾶν δὲ ὃ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως ἁμαρτία ἐστίν.
records.gloss: But the [one] doubting if he eats has been condemned, because not of faith; and everything that not of faith sin is.
pieces: But anyone who has doubts and eats anyway stands condemned, because the eating does not come from faith. Whatever does not come from faith is sin.

L.23: But the one who doubts, if {{gender:they eat|he eats}}, has been condemned, because [it is] not from faith; and everything that [is] not from faith is sin.

R.23: But if people are not sure something is right, and they eat it anyway, they are condemned, because they are not acting from faith. And anything we do that does not come from faith is sin.

decisions.choice: doubts: is divided in mind, not sure that eating is allowed
decisions.reason: διακρίνω is to waver between two views; the same verb says that Abraham did not waver (4:20). This person eats while not convinced that God allows it.

decisions.choice: condemned: guilty before God for acting against conscience
alternatives: condemned only by one's own conscience
decisions.reason: The perfect tense says the person stands condemned. Set beside God's judgment seat (verse 10), it is most naturally God's verdict on doing what one believes to be wrong, though one's own conscience joins in.

decisions.choice: whatever a believer does without the conviction that God approves it is sin
alternatives: every act of a person without faith in Christ is sin, a general statement about all human action
decisions.reason: In context "faith" is the conviction of verse 22, and the sentence closes the argument about food: to act against one's conscience is sin even when the act itself is allowed. Many readers have also taken it as a wider statement about all action done apart from faith in God. The sentence can bear both, but Paul's argument here concerns believers and their conscience.

decisions.choice: the chapter ends here; the closing doxology stands at 16:25-27
alternatives: many later manuscripts place the doxology (16:25-27) after this verse
some manuscripts have it both here and at the end of chapter 16
decisions.reason: The closing doxology of Romans is found at different places in the manuscripts: after 14:23 in many later ones, after 15:33 in one early papyrus, at the end of chapter 16 in the earliest, and in some in two places or not at all. The SBLGNT prints it at 16:25-27. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: anyway
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "anyway" to bring out that the person eats in spite of doubts.

decisions.choice: the eating does not come from faith
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves out the subject; it is the act of eating.
